nameStory: This shrub gets its name from its leaves, which look remarkably similar to those of alder trees - oval-shaped with prominent veins and serrated edges. The 'buckthorn' part comes from its family relationship to other buckthorns, though ironically this species lacks the thorns that give the group its name!
description: Alderleaf buckthorn is a small, thornless shrub that typically grows 2-4 feet tall in New England's wetlands and forests. It has simple, oval leaves with toothed edges that strongly resemble alder leaves, arranged alternately along slender branches. The shrub produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers in spring, followed by small dark berries in late summer. Unlike its thorny relatives, this gentle shrub is completely smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with fine teeth along the edges and prominent parallel veins running from midrib to margin - they feel smooth and thin, just like alder leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing shrub, rarely over 4 feet tall, with smooth branches that feel soft to the touch - no thorns or prickles anywhere on the plant

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish-yellow flowers in small clusters, each flower only about 1/8 inch across with 5 petals - easy to miss unless you look closely

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small round berries that start green and ripen to dark purple-black, about 1/4 inch across and slightly bitter to taste

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on older stems, with younger twigs having a reddish tint - feels smooth under your fingers

habitat: Look for alderleaf buckthorn in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests, especially in swampy areas, stream borders, and wet woodland edges. It thrives in rich, organic soils and is often found growing alongside ferns, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants in partially shaded to shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: Small greenish flowers appear in May, tucked in clusters along the branches. New leaves emerge bright green with very prominent veining.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are at their fullest, showing the characteristic alder-like shape and venation pattern. Green berries begin forming after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and berries ripen to dark purple-black. The fruit becomes most noticeable as leaves begin to thin.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show smooth bark and small buds. Persistent dried berries may remain on branches, and the thornless twigs are distinctive.

funFact: Despite being called a 'buckthorn,' this species is the pacifist of its family - it's completely thornless while most of its relatives are armed with sharp spines, making it the only buckthorn you can grab without getting poked!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young alder trees due to the nearly identical leaf shape and venation. Remember: alders grow near water as trees or large shrubs and have cone-like fruits, while alderleaf buckthorn stays small and produces berries. If it's under 4 feet tall with berries, it's the buckthorn!
contextualKnowledge: The name 'buckthorn' can be misleading since this species lacks thorns entirely. Many buckthorns are considered invasive in New England, but alderleaf buckthorn is a native species that belongs in our ecosystems and provides food for wildlife.
compareHints: Unlike its notorious relative common buckthorn (an invasive species), alderleaf buckthorn is native, thornless, and stays much smaller - rarely exceeding 4 feet tall. Common buckthorn has thorns, grows larger, and has more oval leaves that aren't as strongly veined. Alderleaf buckthorn also prefers wetter sites while common buckthorn tolerates drier areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common buckthorn differs from its native cousin alderleaf buckthorn by having thorny branches (alderleaf buckthorn is thornless) and oval leaves (versus the more rounded, alder-like leaves of the native species).
